clue.text: Somewhat before all, I fear for actual human existence

indicators.note: 'Somewhat' means a part and not the whole, so only a stretch of the words that follow is taken.

parts.note: an unbroken run of letters beginning two into 'before' and stopping two into 'fear'

explanation.surface: A nervous speaker owning up: in front of everybody, they are frightened.
explanation.walkthrough: Word breaks and commas are invisible to a buried answer; this run crosses three of them. 'Fear' gives up only its opening FE, which is why the join reads as ordinary punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: Real life is the ordinary world people actually live in, the thing set against fiction, theory or a screen.

clue.text: Fail to meet expectations in car venue: hide abroad

indicators.note: 'Abroad' means away from home and scattered about, so the letters are no longer where they belong.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: Someone going to ground overseas, stashed out of sight in a car park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction and is only a link word — nothing goes inside anything here. The fodder is the whole of 'car venue hide', twelve letters for a twelve-letter light.
explanation.definitionFit: To underachieve is to perform below what your ability promised, which is exactly falling short of what was expected.

clue.text: One with liability at first demanding extremely broad terms of reference

indicators.note: 'At first' points to the opening of a word, so only the leading letter of each word named is taken.

parts.words: demanding extremely broad terms of reference
parts.note: initials of Demanding Extremely Broad Terms Of Reference

explanation.surface: A negotiator insisting on the widest possible brief before agreeing to start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' usually orders you to take a word's outer letters; here it is just another word donating its initial. Six words follow the instruction and the light is six letters long.
explanation.definitionFit: A debtor is the person who owes the money, so the liability sits on their side of the ledger.

clue.text: A church feature, high, or long?

parts.note: the clue's own opening 'A' is the first letter
the spire is the high feature of a church

explanation.surface: A question about church architecture: is the feature a tall one or a long one?
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' reads as an article and is really a letter of the answer — setters lean on that because 'a' vanishes into any surface. The question mark warns that 'long' is wanted as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire is to yearn and reach for something, which is what 'long' means when it is a verb rather than a measurement.

clue.text: Ricochet reduced line darts players must stay behind

definitions.text: line darts players must stay behind

indicators.note: 'Reduced' means cut down to less than the whole, so what is left is a shorter run inside the word given.

parts.note: an unbroken run of four letters starting at the third letter of this word

explanation.surface: A dart bouncing off the wire and skidding back across the throwing line.
explanation.walkthrough: The oche is the raised strip on the floor of a darts match that a thrower's foot must not cross. It is said 'ockey', which is why it looks so unfamiliar written down.
explanation.definitionFit: The oche is precisely that throwing line — the marked limit a darts player has to stay behind.

clue.text: Meeting Irishman before church

indicators.note: 'Before' fixes the order of the two pieces: what comes before the church goes in front of it.

parts.note: Sean is the crossword's standard Irish forename
CE = Church of England

explanation.surface: An Irishman turning up at the church ahead of everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: CE for the Church of England is worth owning outright; setters write plain 'church' for it without further signal. Sean is their default Irishman, alongside Pat and Erin.
explanation.definitionFit: A seance is a sitting — a group gathered round a table for a session — so 'meeting' covers it plainly.

clue.text: Mark, 100, ultimately superlative — hard to get

indicators.note: 'Ultimately' means at the very end, so only the final letter of the word it governs is taken.

parts.note: a scar is the mark a wound leaves
C is the Roman hundred
the last letter of superlativE

explanation.surface: A report on an exam: a mark of 100, the best there is, and rarely achieved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' leads the word it governs instead of trailing it, which is unusual enough to read past. Roman numerals are standing crossword currency: C a hundred, D five hundred, M a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: Something scarce is in short supply, and the definition names the consequence of that shortage rather than the shortage itself.

clue.text: Old-fashioned aunt, idle, vain, unfortunately

indicators.note: 'Unfortunately' marks things going wrong, and letters that have gone wrong are no longer in their proper order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: A brisk and unkind summary of a relative: lazy, self-regarding and behind the times.
explanation.walkthrough: Adverbs ending in -ly are the commonest hiding place for an anagram signal, because they pass as ordinary comment. The list of insults reads as a sentence and is really a bag of twelve letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Antediluvian means from before Noah's flood, and is used of anything hopelessly out of date — old-fashioned at full strength.

clue.text: Escape group of ships? Not entirely

indicators.note: not entirely means the word is left incomplete, losing its last letter

parts.note: a fleet is a group of ships

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a convoy can get away, then hedges the question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely' cuts the final T from FLEET.
explanation.definitionFit: To flee is to run away, and escape works as the same verb.

clue.text: A number sorted tent hire

indicators.note: 'Sorted' is a rearranging word: things put into a new arrangement no longer stand in the order they arrived in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A festival organiser reporting that the renting of the tents has been dealt with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sorted' reads as 'seen to' in the surface and as 'reordered' in the wordplay. 'A number' names only the category, so the fodder does every bit of the deciding.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirteen is a number, and naming the class rather than the value is fair because the anagram fixes which number is meant.

clue.text: Democrat is eager for changing conflict

indicators.note: the word eager is up for changing, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A US Democrat is keen to switch sides in a dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eager for changing' reads as keenness to switch, but 'for changing' is the anagram signal on 'eager'.
explanation.definitionFit: To conflict is to clash or differ, which is what people who disagree do; both are verbs here.

clue.text: Envied on regular basis period before festival

indicators.note: Doing something on a regular basis is doing it at fixed intervals, so letters are picked at a fixed step through the word.

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of EnViEd

explanation.surface: A person envied at steady intervals during the run-up to a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regular' most often points at the even letters; here it is the odd ones, and only counting settles which. Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve are the everyday proof of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An eve is the day or evening immediately before a feast day, as in Christmas Eve or All Hallows' Eve.

clue.text: Urgent order to abandon court

indicators.note: the word for order must abandon, or give up, the court letters

parts.note: to direct someone is to order them

explanation.surface: A pressing instruction tells someone to leave a courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to abandon' takes CT (court) out of DIRECT. 'Urgent order' reads as one phrase, but 'Urgent' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dire can mean extremely serious and calling for prompt action, as in dire need, so urgent.

clue.text: Store, maybe, source of verbal accounts?

definitions.note: A store is one kind of the thing rather than the whole class, and 'maybe' is the setter's flag that the definition is by example.
definitions.meaning: first definition: a shop is one of these

indicators.note: 'Maybe' warns that what stands beside it is only one instance of the answer, not a synonym for it.

definitions.meaning: second definition: to retail a tale is to pass it on by mouth

explanation.surface: A shop described as the place where all the local gossip starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retail' carries an older second sense: to retail a story is to repeat it around, which makes the teller one of these. 'Accounts' pulls hard towards shop bookkeeping and means stories.
explanation.definitionFit: A retailer sells to the public, so a store is one; and to retail a tale is to recount it, making a retailer a source of spoken accounts.

clue.text: Confusion mostly hard to co-ordinate

parts.note: MESS, meaning confusion, mostly: the last S is left off
H is the pencil grade for hard

explanation.surface: A muddle that is difficult to bring into any kind of order.
explanation.walkthrough: H for hard comes off the side of a pencil, the same convention that gives B for black. The surface reads 'mostly hard' as one phrase, hiding the fact that 'mostly' belongs to the word in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Gears mesh when their teeth fit together, and plans mesh when they are co-ordinated so that each one fits the next.

clue.text: Determined loser coming back, urging tremendous effort initially

indicators.note: coming back means the word loser is read in the opposite direction
initially takes the first letter of each of the three words before it

parts.note: the three words whose first letters are taken

explanation.surface: A beaten competitor returns, spurred on to try very hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming back' turns LOSER into RESOL, and 'initially' adds UTE, the first letters of 'urging tremendous effort'.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolute means firmly set on a purpose, as is someone determined.

clue.text: To some degree, despicable person, the woman

parts.note: a rat is a treacherous, despicable person
'her' stands in for the woman

explanation.surface: A grudging verdict on a woman: somewhat of a nasty piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To some degree' looks like a hedge softening the insult and is in fact the whole definition. Pronouns are stock charade material — 'the woman' is HER or SHE, 'the man' HIM or HE.
explanation.definitionFit: Rather means to a moderate extent: 'rather good' is good to some degree but not wholly.

clue.text: Trim wood

definitions.meaning: first definition: neat and smart in appearance
second definition: an evergreen conifer and the timber it yields

explanation.surface: A carpenter cutting a length of timber down to size.
explanation.walkthrough: Two-word clues are almost always two definitions, and the shorter the clue the safer that bet. 'Trim' is wanted as an adjective meaning neat, not as the verb the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: Spruce means neat and well turned out, as in 'spruce up'; it is also a common evergreen conifer, so 'wood' names both the tree and its timber.

clue.text: One opposing aim — nothing right!

parts.note: an object is an aim or purpose
O is nothing, the zero
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A flat dismissal of somebody's plan: there is nothing right about the aim at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' is an aim in the sense of 'the object of the exercise', and it also means to oppose, so the first piece quietly echoes the definition. O for nothing and R for right are among the busiest single letters in the craft.
explanation.definitionFit: An objector is the person who raises the objection, so the definition names them by the thing they do.

clue.text: Dance sphere

definitions.meaning: first definition: a formal dancing party
second definition: any perfectly round object

explanation.surface: The world of dance, spoken of as a field with borders of its own.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase, 'dance sphere' sounds like a field of activity; the two words are separate definitions with nothing joining them. The dancing sense and the round one are unrelated in origin, which is why each can be clued straight.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball is a formal dance, the kind with an orchestra and a dress code, and it is also any sphere, from a football to a ball of wool.

clue.text: Twisted evil mask

indicators.note: Something twisted has been wrenched out of its proper shape, and letters wrenched about no longer read as they did.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 4 letters

explanation.surface: A grotesque carnival mask contorted into a wicked expression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mask' works as a verb as well as a noun, so the definition stays ambiguous until a crossing settles it. Four-letter anagrams slip past because the fodder looks like an ordinary adjective doing surface work.
explanation.definitionFit: A veil is hung over a face so it cannot be seen, which is the concealing job a mask does.

clue.text: Claim everything, say, aggressive at the end

indicators.note: 'At the end' names the final position, so the closing letter of the word beside it is the one taken.

parts.note: everything is all
'say' introduces an example, and eg is the abbreviation for that
the last letter of aggressivE

explanation.surface: An account of a man who demanded the lot and turned nasty by the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is one of the busiest words in cryptics: it can mean EG, flag a homophone, or stand for a spoken remark. Here it is the two-letter abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To allege is to assert something that has not yet been proved, which is what making a claim means.

clue.text: Drink cartel out of order

indicators.note: Something out of order is not standing in its proper sequence, so the letters are resequenced.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

explanation.surface: A price-fixing ring accused of behaving badly over the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of order' carries its British sense of misbehaving in the surface and its literal sense in the wordplay. The drink wanted is the British name for red Bordeaux, used here as a plain word for red wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Claret is red Bordeaux, and in Britain the word does duty for red wine generally — a drink.
